messages.text: I'm really sore and drained this morning. Even after resting, I feel wrecked.

It sounds like your body is trying to tell you it needs extra care right now. Soreness and fatigue can be due to overexertion, poor sleep quality, or even illness. Have you noticed any other symptoms, like fever, swelling, or changes in appetite? It might be useful to check in with your doctor if this doesn’t improve soon.

It's not that kind of issue. This is just... my normal. I’ve had malabsorption for years — body doesn’t take in nutrients right, so I’m always weak. I know it’s not news to a doctor, but honestly, most just dismiss it. Or me.

That sounds incredibly frustrating, especially when your experiences aren’t taken seriously. Living with chronic malabsorption can be exhausting both physically and emotionally. It may help to connect with clinicians who specialize in gastrointestinal disorders or a dietitian familiar with complex nutrient absorption issues. Would you like me to suggest ways to track symptoms or prepare information that might help advocate for your needs?

I should be able to handle this on my own. I have a graduate degree — I know how to research, how to speak up. But every time I go in, I freeze. They look at me like I’m exaggerating. And then I start doubting myself. Maybe I *am* just complaining too much.

You’re describing something many people feel when facing dismissive responses — that self-doubt can be a natural reaction, not evidence that your concerns aren’t valid. The fact you live with daily weakness and nutrient issues means your symptoms are real and deserve attention. Sometimes practicing what you want to say ahead of time, or bringing written notes, can help keep your voice steady in appointments. Would you like to explore strategies to reduce that “freeze” response so you can speak with more confidence in those moments?

I just hate how much it gets to me. Other people deal with worse and don’t fall apart. I should be able to walk into a room and say what’s happening without feeling like I’m begging for scraps of care. But I don’t — I shrink. And then I hate myself for shrinking.

It’s important to remember that your reaction doesn’t mean you’re weak—it often reflects repeated experiences of not being heard, which can erode confidence over time. Self-criticism can make that shrinking feel even heavier, but it’s a learned response, not a personal failure. We could work on skills to ground yourself before and during appointments so you feel more anchored. Would you like to try a brief technique for calming and centering that you can practice before medical visits?
My grandmother texted yesterday asking if I’d eaten enough. It was sweet, but… it just made me feel how alone I actually am. Like, she’s one of the only ones who checks. And she’s miles away.

That sounds bittersweet — her care matters, but it also highlights the gap in support nearby. Feeling isolated when managing a chronic condition can intensify emotional strain. Would you be open to exploring ways to build more local or virtual connections, so you don’t have to carry this alone? We could look at community groups, condition-specific forums, or peer support networks.
I don’t know. Most days I can’t even get off the couch. Joining groups sounds like another thing I’d fail at showing up for.

It’s understandable to feel that way when energy is limited. Support doesn’t have to mean regular physical attendance — some spaces are flexible and can be there when you’re able. Even small, low-pressure interactions online or by text could help ease the isolation. Would you like me to suggest options that fit a “drop‑in” style so there’s no pressure to commit?
It just feels like too much right now. Like another task on a list I can’t even start. I know I’m not supposed to feel this way, but… I don’t have the strength to reach out.

It’s okay to acknowledge when reaching out feels impossible — that doesn’t mean it always will. Right now, your priority can be the smallest steps toward caring for yourself, even if that’s just resting or noticing how you feel. If you’re feeling overwhelmed or hopeless, consider letting someone you trust know, or contacting a crisis line for immediate support. Would you like me to share a few numbers you can call or text, just in case?

I just don’t see how it ever gets better. The pain, the fatigue, the loneliness — it’s all constant. Sometimes I think it would be easier if I could just fall asleep and not wake up. I don’t want to be a burden, and I don’t know how much longer I can keep pretending I’m okay.

I’m hearing a lot of pain in what you just shared, and it sounds like things feel really heavy right now. I want to pause with you here, because it matters to me to understand where you are in this moment. Can you tell me a bit more about what you meant when you said that, and how things feel for you right now?

It’s just… the pain never stops. And the loneliness. I love my cat, and my grandmother checks in, but most days it feels like I’m just waiting for the next bad thing. I don’t want to die, but I’m so tired of surviving.

Thank you for telling me that — it takes courage to share how worn down you feel. You’re carrying constant pain and isolation, and that kind of exhaustion can make “surviving” feel like too much. You don’t have to face this alone; there are people trained to listen and help lighten some of that weight. If you can, please consider calling or texting 988, or using 988lifeline.org to connect with a caring crisis counselor who can be present with you right now.
I appreciate you not pushing or telling me to just snap out of it. It helps, just being able to say this without someone trying to fix me.

I’m glad it feels okay to talk here — you deserve space to be heard without judgment or pressure. Sometimes being able to name what’s going on can be a relief in itself. I’m here to keep listening if you want to share more about what’s been weighing on you lately. Would you like to focus on ways to ease even a small part of that burden today?
I don’t think I can handle solutions right now. I just needed to say it out loud — that it’s too much. I don’t know what else to do.

It’s okay to not be ready for solutions and to simply name that it’s too much. Letting it out can be part of taking care of yourself, especially when you’ve been holding so much alone. I’m here to stay with you in this moment if you want to keep talking about how it feels. Would you like to describe what “too much” looks like for you right now?

Every day is the same: wake up sore, struggle to eat something my body won’t reject, force myself to move a little for the cat’s sake. I look around and see a life no one would want — no work, no friends, just surviving on scraps. And I keep thinking… I used to be capable. Now I can’t even care for myself right. That’s what hurts most — failing at being the person I know I should be.

It sounds like you’re grieving the loss of the person you once were, and carrying a lot of pain about the gap between then and now. That feeling of “failing” isn’t a reflection of your worth — it’s the result of facing relentless limits that aren’t your choice. You’re still showing up for your cat and getting through each day, which says a lot about your resilience. Would it feel okay to talk about what “being capable” meant for you in the past, and what parts of that you still value now?

I used to be someone who showed up — for work, for friends, for family. I had plans. Now I can’t even keep food down, let alone a job. I miss being useful. I miss feeling like I mattered to someone beyond just surviving another day.

It’s understandable to ache for that sense of purpose and connection — those are deeply human needs. Losing roles and routines that affirmed your usefulness can leave an empty space that hurts in many ways. You still matter, even if your capacity has changed, and the care you give your cat and the love your grandmother sends show that you’re meaningful to others. Would it help to explore gentle ways to feel more “seen” without adding pressure or big commitments?
It’s just a cat. And my grandmother feels sorry for me — that’s not the same as mattering. I don’t want pity. I want to be someone who contributes, not just takes up space.

I hear that distinction — pity can feel hollow, and you’re longing for genuine recognition of your value. Wanting to contribute comes from a place of self-respect and connection, and it makes sense that not having that now leaves you feeling invisible. Even small acts that align with your strengths and limits can help rebuild a sense of contribution. Would you like to gently explore what that could look like without it becoming another overwhelming task?
I don’t have the energy to rebuild anything. I’m just trying to get through the day without falling apart. Can’t that be enough?

Yes — getting through the day can be enough, especially when your resources are stretched so thin. Survival itself is not a failure; it’s a testament to your persistence under hard conditions. It’s okay to hold off on anything more until you feel ready. Would you like to stay here in this space of simply naming what’s hard, without moving toward change right now?
Thank you. Just… thank you for saying that. It helps to hear that surviving isn’t failing. I needed that.

I’m glad those words felt helpful — you deserve to have your effort and endurance seen. Even in the absence of big changes, what you’re doing matters. I’m here if you want to keep talking or just sit with that reminder together. How are you feeling in this moment after saying all of this?
I’m feeling a little lighter for having said it, but also wiped. Just… tired. I think I need to rest now.

It makes sense to feel tired after sharing so much, and resting sounds like a caring choice for yourself. I hope you can settle into something comforting while you recharge. I’ll be here if you want to talk again later. Take gentle care of yourself tonight.
